title: Slow-cooker mushroom bourguignon
subtitle: A rich, deeply flavoured plant-based take on the French classic
excerpt: Chestnut mushrooms braised in red wine with carrot, onion, and herbs. Deeply flavoured and better the next day. Vegan and naturally gluten-free.
sourceNotes: Mushroom bourguignon is a plant-based adaptation of the French beef bourguignon, popularised by writers including Ina Garten and Deb Perelman (Smitten Kitchen). The slow-cooker method draws on the long-braising technique at the heart of the original.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The flavour improves overnight. Make the day before and reheat gently before serving.

content.text: The dried porcini mushrooms are the key to this dish. They bring a deep, savoury quality that holds its own against the red wine. Add them whole or crumbled directly into the pot; they will rehydrate in the cooking liquid and soften completely.
Use a wine you would drink. Cheap cooking wine adds a harsh note that the long cook does not fully soften. A good, affordable table red works perfectly.
Serve over mashed potato, creamy polenta, or buttered noodles. A handful of fresh parsley at the end adds freshness.

Add {{mushrooms-chestnut}} of chestnut mushrooms and {{mushrooms-porcini-dried}} of dried porcini to the slow cooker. Add {{carrot}} of carrot chunks, {{onion}} sliced onions, and {{garlic}} of crushed garlic. Stir in {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree. Pour over {{red-wine}} of red wine and {{stock-vegetable}} of vegetable stock. Tuck in {{thyme}} of thyme sprigs and {{bay-leaves}} of bay. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper-ground}} of pepper.

Set the slow cooker to LOW and cook for 5 to 6 hours. The mushrooms will reduce in volume and the sauce will darken. In the last 30 minutes, stir in the cornflour slurry and switch to HIGH. The sauce will thicken as it heats. Discard the thyme sprigs and bay leaves before serving.

rows.cause: The alcohol from the wine did not fully cook off during the slow cook.
rows.fix: Switch to HIGH with the lid off for 20 minutes to drive off the remaining alcohol. Stir in a teaspoon of tomato puree to mellow the flavour.

rows.cause: Mushrooms are mostly water. They release all of it during cooking and reduce significantly in size.
rows.fix: This is normal. The flavour transfers into the sauce. Starting with 600g of fresh mushrooms gives a good ratio of mushroom to sauce after cooking.

rows.cause: The mushrooms released more liquid than the cornflour absorbed.
rows.fix: Add a second tablespoon of cornflour slurry and cook on HIGH for 15 more minutes. Or reduce the sauce in a pan separately.

rows.cause: The dried porcini were left out, or the wine was very cheap.
rows.fix: Stir in a tablespoon of soy sauce, which adds savouriness without tasting of soy. A teaspoon of balsamic vinegar also helps.

content.text: Boeuf bourguignon is one of the most celebrated dishes in French cooking. The mushroom version takes the same technique and applies it to an ingredient that is well suited to long braising. Chestnut mushrooms have enough body to hold their shape. Dried porcini do the work that beef marbling does in the original. The result is not a lesser version of the classic; it is its own dish.
